item.title: By: Carl
item.dc:creator: Carl
item.description:
<strong>Make 'em yourself Kale Chips</strong> Chop 9-10 pounds of kale into 1" strips (more or less) Fine chop 6-8oz fresh ginger, 1/8" Cut off heel end from 6-8 bulbs of fresh garlic, break into cloves. In Cuisinart mixer add:
1-1/2 cup soy sauce, 2 Tsp chilli flakes 2 Tsp black pepper Chopped ginger and garlic cloves. (Optional: nutritional yeast 1-2 cups)
Blend for 5 minutes or so, Add 1 cup peanut butter Blend for 5 minutes or so,
Add the sauce (contents of Cuisinart) to chopped kale. Kneed well with both hand vigorously until sauce is distributed throughout the kale
Place in a solar dryer in an inch thick layer (or other means of drying) for a day or more (depending on your climate) until crisp . Note: sunlight shouldn't shine on the chips themselves.
If kale chips absorb moisture (i.e., in winter), use silica gel to remove moisture, and/or place in oven (not turned on… only pilot light on) for a day or so. I keep a few silica gel canisters with the kale in winter and 'recharge' the silica gel in the oven a few times during winter.
item.content:encoded:
Make ’em yourself Kale Chips
Chop 9-10 pounds of kale into 1″ strips (more or less)
Fine chop 6-8oz fresh ginger, 1/8″
Cut off heel end from 6-8 bulbs of fresh garlic, break into cloves.
In Cuisinart mixer add:

1-1/2 cup soy sauce,
2 Tsp chilli flakes
2 Tsp black pepper
Chopped ginger and garlic cloves.
(Optional: nutritional yeast 1-2 cups)

Blend for 5 minutes or so,
Add 1 cup peanut butter
Blend for 5 minutes or so,

Add the sauce (contents of Cuisinart) to chopped kale.
Kneed well with both hand vigorously until sauce is distributed throughout the kale

Place in a solar dryer in an inch thick layer (or other means of drying) for a day or more (depending on your climate) until crisp . Note: sunlight shouldn’t shine on the chips themselves.

If kale chips absorb moisture (i.e., in winter), use silica gel to remove moisture, and/or place in oven (not turned on… only pilot light on) for a day or so. I keep a few silica gel canisters with the kale in winter and ‘recharge’ the silica gel in the oven a few times during winter.

item.title: By: Jessica
item.dc:creator: Jessica
item.description: Kale is lovely in soup, and cooked and chopped it makes a great addition to a fritatta. If you destem it and cut it into slender ribbons, then knead it, raw, with lots of good olive oil and some salt, it makes a wonderful salad ingredient. It breaks down a bit and becomes succulent, meaty and delicious. Great with broccoli raab, grated carrot and avocado chunks plus your favorite olive-oil or tahini-based salad dressing.

item.title: By: carl
item.dc:creator: carl
item.content:encoded:
Look closely and you’ll see how much more nutritious kale is over pac choy, except for fola (folic acid) where pac choy beat kale hands down. The moral of this is the importance of some variety. Each food has its strong points. It is just that kale has so many strong points! By the way, I left the RDA column amount in as a reference, but the comparison is just between 3.5oz (100g.) of kale and pac choy. It should be said too that pac choy is a mighty healthy vegi. It just looks weak when judged against kale.

Now, speaking of availability in the market. I happened to see kale at the market last year and was blown away by the price. As I recall they charged close to $5 a bunch (about a plant). It is easy to be a rich person if you measure wealth in how much kale you can grow. It is the easiest and most prolific. So why do they charge so much? I suppose it is just a case of supply and demand. Little demand makes for little supply which increases the price for those rare persons who buy kale. Interesting.

item.description:
I'm sold. I don't think it's always available at the market so I guess it's best to grow it yourself.
I've always heard that bok choy is the most nutritious vegetable...maybe I'll try to find a comparison.
